# Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

We examine the distribution of job satisfaction, its development from 2004 to 2024, and differences across occupations, demographic groups, employment arrangements and economic periods. All figures use **unweighted respondent-year observations** from the employed sample unless otherwise stated. Because respondents can appear in several years, these plots describe the sample rather than independent individuals. Statistical tests are discussed separately in the Analysis section.

## Univariate Analysis

### Distribution of job satisfaction

```{python}
#| label: fig-job-satisfaction-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of reported job satisfaction among employed respondents, 2004–2024."
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from IPython.display import display

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
scores = employed_sample["JOB_SATISFACTION"].dropna()
ax.hist(scores, bins=np.arange(-0.5, 11.5, 1), edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(scores.mean(), linestyle="--", color="black", label=f"Mean: {scores.mean():.2f}")
ax.set(xlabel="Job satisfaction (0–10)", ylabel="Respondent-year observations", xticks=range(11))
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

As shown in @fig-job-satisfaction-distribution, job satisfaction is concentrated toward the upper end of the 0–10 scale, with a median of **8**. The distribution is not symmetric: relatively few respondents report very low satisfaction. For this reason, we examine both the mean and the percentage reporting **low satisfaction (0–5)** rather than relying on the mean alone.

### Summary statistics and potential outliers

```{python}
#| label: tbl-eda-summary-statistics
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics for job satisfaction and age in the employed analysis sample."
summary_stats = analysis_sample[["JOB_SATISFACTION", "AGE"]].agg(
    ["count", "mean", "std", "median", "min", "max"]
).T.rename(columns={"count": "N", "mean": "Mean", "std": "SD", "median": "Median", "min": "Minimum", "max": "Maximum"})
display(summary_stats.round(2))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-job-satisfaction-box
#| fig-cap: "Box plot of job satisfaction scores (0–10); extreme responses are retained as valid survey answers."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.3))
sns.boxplot(x=scores, ax=ax, color="lightsteelblue")
ax.set(xlabel="Job satisfaction (0–10)", xlim=(-0.5, 10.5), xticks=range(11))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

@tbl-eda-summary-statistics reports the central tendency and spread of the two continuous variables used in the project. The distribution in @fig-job-satisfaction-box is bounded by the questionnaire's 0–10 scale and is concentrated toward high satisfaction. Values at the low end can appear as statistical outliers in a box plot, but **they are valid survey responses, not data errors**, so we do not remove them. The bounded, uneven distribution also motivates reporting medians and the low-satisfaction share alongside means. The subsequent regressions use respondent-clustered standard errors because individuals can contribute several observations.

## Bivariate Analysis

### Overall trend in job satisfaction

```{python}
#| label: fig-annual-satisfaction
#| fig-cap: "Annual unweighted mean job satisfaction, 2004–2024."
annual = (employed_sample.assign(LOW_SAT=employed_sample["JOB_SATISFACTION"].le(5))
          .groupby("YEAR", as_index=False)
          .agg(mean_satisfaction=("JOB_SATISFACTION", "mean"),
               low_satisfaction=("LOW_SAT", "mean")))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
ax.plot(annual["YEAR"], annual["mean_satisfaction"], marker="o", markersize=3)
ax.set(xlabel="Survey year", ylabel="Mean satisfaction (0–10)")
ax.set_xticks([2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2024])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
display(annual.loc[annual["YEAR"].isin([2004, 2024])].round(3))
```

As shown in @fig-annual-satisfaction, the unweighted mean fell from **8.212 in 2004** to **7.815 in 2024**, a decline of **0.397 points**. The percentage reporting low satisfaction rose from **6.27%** to **7.56%**. These are descriptive trends and may partly reflect changes in the respondents included each year.

### Occupational differences (RQ1.1)

```{python}
#| label: fig-occupation-satisfaction
#| fig-cap: "Mean job satisfaction by civilian occupational group, pooled across 2004–2024."
occupation_labels = {
    1: "Managers", 2: "Professionals", 3: "Technicians", 4: "Clerical support",
    5: "Service and sales", 6: "Agricultural", 7: "Craft workers",
    8: "Machine operators", 9: "Elementary occupations"
}
occ = employed_sample.loc[employed_sample["OCCUPATION"].isin(occupation_labels)].copy()
occ["Occupation"] = occ["OCCUPATION"].map(occupation_labels)
occ_summary = (occ.groupby("Occupation")["JOB_SATISFACTION"]
               .agg(["mean", "count"]).sort_values("mean"))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.barh(occ_summary.index, occ_summary["mean"])
ax.set(xlabel="Mean satisfaction (0–10)", ylabel="")
ax.set_xlim(0, 10)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

As shown in @fig-occupation-satisfaction, average satisfaction differs across occupational groups. Agricultural workers have the highest pooled average, while clerical support workers have the lowest among the nine civilian groups. We exclude Armed Forces (ISCO 0) from this comparison because of its small sample. Differences in occupation may overlap with age, region and employment arrangements; the Analysis section tests adjusted associations.

### Demographic and employment differences (RQ1.1)

```{python}
#| label: tbl-demographic-satisfaction
#| tbl-cap: "Mean job satisfaction by age group, sex and employment arrangement."
eda_demo = analysis_sample.copy()
eda_demo["Age group"] = pd.cut(
    eda_demo["AGE"], bins=[0, 24, 34, 44, 54, 64, np.inf],
    labels=["Under 25", "25–34", "35–44", "45–54", "55–64", "65+"],
    include_lowest=True
)
eda_demo["Sex"] = eda_demo["SEX"].map({1: "Men", 2: "Women"})
eda_demo["Employment arrangement"] = eda_demo["EMPLOYMENT_STATUS"].map({
    1: "Full-time (37+ hours)", 2: "Part-time (5–36 hours)",
    3: "Part-time (1–4 hours)", 5: "Family business"
})
for label in ["Age group", "Sex", "Employment arrangement"]:
    summary = (eda_demo.dropna(subset=[label])
               .groupby(label, observed=True)["JOB_SATISFACTION"]
               .agg(Observations="count", Mean="mean"))
    print(f"\n{label}")
    display(summary.round(3))
```

The group summaries in @tbl-demographic-satisfaction show that satisfaction generally increases in older age groups, although these are comparisons across respondents, not evidence that aging causes higher satisfaction. Women report a slightly higher pooled mean than men. Very short part-time work and family-business work show higher unadjusted averages than full-time work, but their sample sizes are much smaller. The employment-arrangement comparison includes only records with the relevant valid categories. **Region is region of residence**, not necessarily workplace location. The regional descriptive comparison is shown next, with adjusted associations reported in the Analysis section.

### Regional differences (RQ1.1)

```{python}
#| label: fig-region-satisfaction
#| fig-cap: "Mean job satisfaction by region of residence, 2004–2024 (unweighted)."
region_labels = {
    1: "Lake Geneva", 2: "Espace Mittelland", 3: "Northwestern Switzerland",
    4: "Zurich", 5: "Eastern Switzerland", 6: "Central Switzerland",
    7: "Ticino"
}
region_data = employed_sample.loc[employed_sample["REGION"].isin(region_labels)].copy()
region_data["Region"] = region_data["REGION"].map(region_labels)
region_summary = (region_data.groupby("Region")["JOB_SATISFACTION"]
                  .agg(Mean="mean", Observations="count")
                  .sort_values("Mean"))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.6))
ax.barh(region_summary.index, region_summary["Mean"], color="steelblue")
ax.set(xlabel="Mean satisfaction (0–10)", ylabel="", xlim=(0, 10))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
display(region_summary.round(3))
```

@fig-region-satisfaction compares the seven **regions of residence**, not workplace locations. The pooled averages show geographic variation in job satisfaction, which could partly reflect differences in workforce composition and employment conditions. This motivates including region as a covariate in the adjusted RQ1.1 model rather than interpreting these descriptive differences as regional effects.

### Changes around economic events (RQ1.2)

```{python}
#| label: fig-event-windows
#| fig-cap: "Mean job satisfaction in the year before, during and after three major economic events."
event_years = {"2009 financial crisis": 2009, "2015 Swiss franc shock": 2015, "2020 COVID-19": 2020}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.8), sharey=True)
for ax, (event, year) in zip(axes, event_years.items()):
    window = annual[annual["YEAR"].between(year - 1, year + 1)]
    ax.plot(window["YEAR"], window["mean_satisfaction"], marker="o")
    ax.set_title(event)
    ax.set_xticks([year - 1, year, year + 1])
    ax.set_xlabel("Year")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Mean satisfaction (0–10)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

As shown in @fig-event-windows, the 2009 window shows a small decline; the 2015 window shows lower satisfaction during and after the franc shock; and 2020 shows a temporary increase followed by a return near the 2019 level in 2021. These windows are **not causal estimates** of the economic events. Respondent-clustered comparisons of the same years appear in the Analysis section.

## Multivariate Analysis

### Occupation across economic periods (RQ1.3)

```{python}
#| label: fig-occupation-period-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Average job satisfaction by occupation and broad economic period."
period_data = occ.copy()
period_data["Economic period"] = pd.cut(
    period_data["YEAR"], bins=[2003, 2008, 2014, 2019, 2024],
    labels=["2004–2008", "2009–2014", "2015–2019", "2020–2024"]
)
period_means = period_data.pivot_table(
    index="Occupation", columns="Economic period", values="JOB_SATISFACTION",
    aggfunc="mean", observed=True
).reindex(list(occupation_labels.values()))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
sns.heatmap(period_means, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="YlGnBu", ax=ax,
            cbar_kws={"label": "Mean satisfaction"})
ax.set(xlabel="Economic period", ylabel="")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

As shown in @fig-occupation-period-heatmap, occupational averages vary across the four broad periods, and the gaps between occupations are not identical in each period. These period labels are descriptive groupings, not four separate crisis treatments. The interaction regression in the Analysis section tests whether occupational differences vary significantly across periods.

## Correlation Analysis and Choice of Visualisations

A conventional correlation matrix across the categorical variables would be misleading: `OCCUPATION`, `SEX`, `REGION`, and `EMPLOYMENT_STATUS` are numeric **codes for categories**, not continuous measurements. A correlation between their numeric codes would depend on the arbitrary numbering of categories. We therefore use group means, grouped comparisons, and the occupation-by-period heatmap instead of an inappropriate correlation heatmap or scatter plot. Relationships involving the continuous variable `AGE` are explored through age groups, which also makes the results easier to interpret for RQ1.1.

## EDA Summary and Implications for Analysis

The figures and tables above indicate a gradual decline in overall satisfaction, differences across occupations and demographic groups, and distinct patterns around the three event windows. The weighted annual-mean check also indicates a decline from 2004 to 2024 (**8.207 to 7.711**), although the report's main EDA remains unweighted. These findings motivate three sets of respondent-clustered regressions: adjusted group comparisons (RQ1.1), before/during/after event-window comparisons (RQ1.2), and an occupation-by-economic-period interaction (RQ1.3). The EDA supports the selection of occupation, age, sex, region, employment arrangement and survey year for RQ1.1; short event windows for RQ1.2; and occupation-by-period interaction terms for RQ1.3. The models and significance tests are presented in the Analysis section. None of these observational comparisons establishes causation.
